Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-25 15:00 UTC | Duration: 45m
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Miguel Torres (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Atlas Head of ML), Daniel Kim (Atlas Infra), Liam O'Connor (Atlas CTO)

Summary: quick run through of this week's benchmark numbers: p50/p95/p99, throughput at target concurrency, memory footprint, and comparison to baseline provider CloudX. A few transcription artefacts present, cf KV cache spelled sometimes K V cache, and Redwood Mini appears as red will mini in a few places.

[00:00] Avery Chen: Hey everyone — thanks for joining, we'll keep to 45. Quick agenda: numbers review, what changed since last week, tuning notes, security asks, next steps. Priya, Daniel, Liam — anything to add?
[00:12] Priya Shah: No, this looks good. We want to focus on tail latency and also the cost delta vs CloudX, because our ops team flagged higher p99s last week.
[00:20] Miguel Torres: Cool, I'll jump into the numbers. We ran the same suite you provided — 1k samples per model, mixed seq lengths (64/256/1024 distribution you sent). Baseline provider CloudX numbers are on tab "baseline" in the sheet I uploaded. Link: drive.google.com/\u2026/atlas-poc-benchmarks (short link).
[00:36] Miguel Torres: For Redwood Hosted (latest branch, Redwood-3B quantized int8-ish) at concurrency 16 we measured: p50 52ms, p95 210ms, p99 490ms, throughput ~42 TPS sustained. Memory per instance ~13GB with KV cache off.
[00:56] Miguel Torres: With KV caching enabled and warm cache on the short prompts, p50 drops to 18ms p95 ~80ms p99 ~230ms, throughput jumps to ~85 TPS at same instance type.
[01:14] Priya Shah: Wait — those p99 numbers look better with KV cache than CloudX? Our baseline showed p99 around 300-350ms with their caching.
[01:22] Miguel Torres: Right — CloudX numbers we saw were p50 60ms p95 240ms p99 330-360ms, throughput ~40 TPS for comparable VM GPUs. So overall Redwood is matching or surpassing on throughput and better on cache-warm tail.
[01:37] Daniel Kim: Can you confirm test harness parity? Our infra engineer said CloudX used slightly higher batch sizes by default which helps throughput but hurts latency.
[01:45] Miguel Torres: Yep, we tried to mimic their defaults but also ran a parity run: batch sizes at 8, 16. In parity run at batch=16 CloudX throughput improved to 55 TPS but p99 increased to ~420ms. Redwood with continuous batching and our kernel selection kept p99 at ~360ms at batch=16. Small transcription note: sometimes "continuous batching" in notes becomes "continuous catching" in the auto transcript.
[02:06] Liam O'Connor: So bottom line — cost per token? If Redwood is faster but p99 still slightly worse in burst scenarios we need to quantify cost tradeoff.
[02:15] Avery Chen: We've modeled cost both ways. In the shared spreadsheet (sheet row "cost-model"), at expected traffic profile (20% burst windows) Redwood Hosted with burst policy is roughly 8-12% cheaper than CloudX at same QoS, Dedicated would be ~20% cheaper once you amortize reserved capacity. We'll send updated price deck.
[02:36] Priya Shah: Dedicated sounds attractive but our compliance team pushes for VPC/private deployment. Any difference in perf?
[02:44] Miguel Torres: Functionally no — performance is tied to instance types. Private deployment adds network overhead if you're calling across peered VPCs, typically <8-12ms added latency. If you deploy within their VPC/on-prem it's negligible. We did an on-prem-like run and saw ~6ms added median.
[03:02] Daniel Kim: Good to know. Also can you confirm KMS options — we need HSM-backed keys for payment PII.
[03:08] Avery Chen: Yes — Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations, and we provide audit logs and tenant-level RBAC. We'll attach SOC 2 + ISO docs; Miguel will point to the compliance packet.
[03:18] Miguel Torres: Quick call-out on tuning: quantization profile matters — int8 reduces mem and improves throughput but sometimes increases tail jitter on longer sequences. For Atlas prompts (lots of short completions) int8 looks safe. Also, prefix/KV caching is huge for repeated context use — saves ~30-60% cost on token-level in our runs.
[03:36] Priya Shah: We saw regressions for some prompts in int8 in a prior test — do you run eval regressions?
[03:42] Miguel Torres: Yes we run evaluation sets against your prompt corpus; quality deltas are in the sheet under "evals". For the handful of failing prompts we recommend the mid-quant profile or per-route float fallback — incurs slight CPU/latency hit but keeps quality.
[03:56] Avery Chen: On the p99 tail — Miguel, can you explain the plan to isolate root cause?
[04:01] Miguel Torres: Sure. Plan: reproduce burst pattern (500 concurrent short requests for 30s), capture tail traces, turn on detailed kernel-level tracing to see whether scheduling or memory GC is the culprit. Then try per-request kv-cache affinity and reduced batch windows. We'll also run a run with different inference kernels (we call it "alternate kernel flow" in notes).
[04:22] Priya Shah: That sounds good. For the run, we need you to use our real prompt set not synthetic — we'll upload the final set after the call.
[04:29] Miguel Torres: Great. Also minor transcript glitch: sometimes "KV cache" is autogenerated as "K V c a ch e" in the export.
[04:36] Daniel Kim: On network side — we'll open the egress window for the test, Daniel to share diagram and rules.
[04:43] Avery Chen: Action items recap in a sec. One question from Liam — if we go Dedicated, how does autoscaling handle sudden spikes?
[04:51] Miguel Torres: Dedicated supports burst pools and configured autoscaling policies. Policy is based on queued requests and token-per-second smoothing. You can set a hard SLO for p50 and a soft SLO for p99 with fallbacks to cheaper model variants if the soft SLO is missed.
[05:07] Liam O'Connor: Fallbacks would be ok as long as we can guarantee no PII leaves the VPC for Private deployments.
[05:13] Avery Chen: Right — private deployments keep everything inside customer's network and control plane; fallback model variants can be deployed as private images too.
[05:20] Priya Shah: A couple of nitpicks on the sheet: can you include the exact GPU types used and driver versions? That matters for kernel performance.
[05:28] Miguel Torres: Absolutely — I added a column for instance type, GPU (e.g., A100-80GB) and driver/runtime. We'll push updated sheet.
[05:35] Priya Shah: Also please include the raw latencies (not summarized) so our SREs can eyeball tail patterns.
[05:41] Miguel Torres: Will do.
[05:44] (brief cross talk)
[05:50] Avery Chen: OK quick recap of next steps and owners — Miguel to run focused p99 burst tests with KV cache and alternate kernels and upload traces (due Friday 2026-03-27). Avery to share pricing and pilot contract template. Daniel to share VPC diagram and firewall rules by Monday. Priya to upload final prompt sets. We'll aim for an on-prem test the week of 2026-04-06.
[06:12] Priya Shah: One more question — competitors: we looked at OpenAI and HF. When we showed OpenAI the prompts the quality looked a touch better on a couple prompts — is that from model differences or tuning?
[06:22] Miguel Torres: Usually model architecture + training data differences; we can reproduce few evals with larger family variants (Redwood-7B) if you want to test quality vs cost tradeoff. That's an explicit next step if you care about those failing prompts.
[06:37] Liam O'Connor: Yes let's do that for 3 failing prompts.
[06:40] Avery Chen: Great. Any other blockers?
[06:43] Daniel Kim: Not from infra. We'll wait for the sheet and traces.
[06:46] Avery Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll share the notes and updated spreadsheet after the call.
[06:50] (meeting ends)
